subject: Existence of simulation studies on categorical/ordered data in lavaan

messages.author: edceb8dce9472a62
messages.subject: Existence of simulation studies on categorical/ordered data in lavaan
parts:
Hi all, 

Reaching out to see if anyone is aware of the existence of formal simulation paper comparing different ways to handle categorical data in lavaan. 

In particular, using simulated data to compare: 
1) declaring ordered and using WLSMV
2) using WLSMV without ordered = c()
3) using blavaan for bayesian
4) using MLR
5) varying the number of levels (e.g., dichotomous vs. 3 level ordered vs. more levels etc.)

Ideally datasets which would lead to significant and nonsignificant thresholds would be used, because I have heard discussion about the adequacy of not using ordered = c() when the thresholds are non-significant.

I have looked for this type of paper many times and never find anything and am considering working on this sort of paper myself. 

Thanks,
Chris

messages.author: 3fe90052fbf2f899
messages.subject: Re: Existence of simulation studies on categorical/ordered data in lavaan
parts: Reaching out to see if anyone is aware of the existence of formal simulation paper comparing different ways to handle categorical data in lavaan.

https://doi.org/10.1080/10705511.2017.1421467

Also ask on SEMNET, there are more people to respond (especially Cam MacIntosh, who is a living database of references)

https://listserv.ua.edu/cgi-bin/wa?SUBED1=semnet&A=1
2) using WLSMV without ordered = c()

That would not make sense.  The procedure is designed for categorical data.  Thresholds and polychoric correlations are estimated first, then the model is fitted to those.  The weight matrix is calculated from the uncertainty of the threshold and polychoric estimates.  If you don't estimate them, what weight matrix would you use?
3) using blavaan for bayesian

blavaan cannot yet handle categorical outcomes.  Ed is working on it, but the computation time is incredibly slow, so it might be a while until he can make a practical solution available.
 
4) using MLR

This one is specifically about testing invariance with missing ordinal data.  It includes a comparison of WLSMV with FIML(R)
https://doi.org/10.1080/00273171.2019.1608799
5) varying the number of levels (e.g., dichotomous vs. 3 level ordered vs. more levels etc.)

In the first paper I linked to, we had 2 or 5 categories.   The second only had 5 categories.  Rhemtulla et al. did a comprehensive simulation study comparing 2, 3, ... 7 categories (also MLR vs. WLSMV), but it was before lavaan could analyze categorical data, so I think she used Mplus or EQS.

http://psychmodels.ucdavis.edu/uploads/8/6/3/9/86398102/rhemtullabrosseauliardsavalei_pm.pdf

In fact, there are many studies comparing WLSMV to MLR, but they typically use Mplus.  lavaan uses the same specifications as Mplus, so they should still be informative for you.

Ideally datasets which would lead to significant and nonsignificant thresholds would be used, because I have heard discussion about the adequacy of not using ordered = c() when the thresholds are non-significant.

I don't know if you simply misunderstood, but a nonsignificant threshold does not mean your data are not categorical.  It just means the proportion of subjects above/below that threshold is not statistically distinguishable from 50/50%.  If you have a binary item with 50% in each category, your threshold will be exactly zero, and you should absolutely still declare it as ordered=.  If anything, you might consider fixing the threshold to zero instead of estimating it, but if that was not an a priori hypothesis, there is no good reason to do that just to avoid a nonsignificant threshold estimate.  The point of thresholds is not to be nonzero (they are not factor loadings).

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen
